concepts: Number of subsets of a finite set
questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be two finite sets with $m$ and $n$ elements respectively. The total number of subsets of the set $A$ is $56$ more than the total number of subsets of $B$. Then the distance of the point $P(m,n)$ from the point $Q(-2,-3)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Write $2^m-2^n=2^n(2^{m-n}-1)=8\cdot 7$ and read off $m$ and $n$.
solution: A set with $m$ elements has $2^m$ subsets, so the given condition is $2^m-2^n=56$.
(Uniqueness: $2^n(2^{m-n}-1)=2^3\cdot 7$; the odd factor $2^{m-n}-1$ must equal $7$, so $n=3$ and $m-n=3$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Pull out the power of $2$: the odd part of $56$ fixes $n$ at once, with no trial of powers.
solution: The factor $2^d-1$ is odd, so all powers of $2$ in $56$ belong to $2^n$: $2^n=2^3$, so $n=3$.
Then $2^d-1=7$, so $2^d=8$ and $d=3$, giving $m=6$.
The vector from $Q(-2,-3)$ to $P(6,3)$ is $(8,6)$, a multiple of the Pythagorean triple $(4,3,5)$.
So $PQ=2\cdot 5=10$, as before.

useful_results: $2^m-2^n=2^n(2^{m-n}-1)$: the odd part $2^{m-n}-1$ and the power of $2$ can be read separately, so the solution is unique.
A set with $k$ elements has $2^k$ subsets, $2^k-1$ non-empty and $2^k-1$ proper subsets.
Recognise Pythagorean triples ($3,4,5$; $5,12,13$; $8,15,17$) to evaluate distances without a calculator: here $(8,6)=2(4,3)$ gives $10$.

concepts: Types of relations: reflexive, symmetric and transitive
questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ if and only if $ad-bc$ is divisible by $5$. Then $R$ is:
options: Reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.answer: (B) Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.key_idea: Test the three properties one by one; for transitivity look for a counterexample using a pair that is $\equiv(0,0)\pmod 5$.
solution: Reflexive: $(a,b)\,R\,(a,b)$ because $ab-ba=0$, which is divisible by $5$. So $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: let $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$, i.e. $ad-bc$ is divisible by $5$.
Then $bc-ad=-(ad-bc)$ is also divisible by $5$, so $(c,d)\,R\,(a,b)$. So $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive: take $(3,1)$, $(10,5)$ and $(1,1)$.
$(3,1)\,R\,(10,5)$ since $3\cdot5-1\cdot10=5$ is divisible by $5$.
$(10,5)\,R\,(1,1)$ since $10\cdot1-5\cdot1=5$ is divisible by $5$.
But $(3,1)\,R\,(1,1)$ would need $3\cdot1-1\cdot1=2$ to be divisible by $5$, which is false. So $R$ is not transitive.
Hence $R$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: $ad-bc\equiv0\pmod5$ says the two vectors are parallel over $\mathbb{Z}_5$; the zero vector is parallel to everything, which breaks transitivity.
solution: Reduce $(a,b)$ modulo $5$: $ad-bc=\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, so $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ means the two vectors are linearly dependent over $\mathbb{Z}_5$.
Every vector is dependent with itself (determinant $0$) and dependence is symmetric, so $R$ is reflexive and symmetric.
The vector $(5,0)\equiv(0,0)$ is dependent with every vector, e.g. with $(1,0)$ and with $(0,1)$.
But $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are not dependent: $1\cdot1-0\cdot0=1$ is not divisible by $5$.
Hence (B).

useful_results: $ad-bc\equiv0\pmod p$ means $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ are proportional over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ (the cross-product / determinant test for parallel vectors).

A relation of the type 'parallel' is an equivalence on non-zero vectors (it has $p+1=6$ classes for $p=5$), but the zero vector is related to everything, so on all of $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ transitivity fails.
To disprove transitivity, look for a 'hub' element related to two unrelated elements; to disprove reflexivity, test $(x,x)$; symmetry usually follows from a symmetric defining formula.

concepts: Equivalence relations: smallest equivalence relation containing given pairs
questions.question: If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $\{(1,2),(1,3)\}\subset R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is:
questions.key_idea: The smallest equivalence relation containing the pairs is obtained by adding exactly the reflexive, symmetric and transitive consequences.
solution: For reflexivity $R$ must contain $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)$.
For symmetry, $(1,2)$ forces $(2,1)$ and $(1,3)$ forces $(3,1)$.
Since $(2,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are in $R$, transitivity forces $(2,3)$; similarly $(3,1)$ and $(1,2)$ force $(3,2)$.
Now $R=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4),(3,2),(2,3),(1,3),(3,1)\}$, and this set is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Every pair added was forced, so $R$ is the smallest such relation and has $10$ elements: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: A smallest equivalence relation is the partition into connected pieces of the graph of the given pairs; its size is the sum of squares of the class sizes.
solution: Join $1-2$ and $1-3$ by edges; element $4$ is untouched.
The equivalence classes are the connected pieces: $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{4\}$.
An equivalence relation with classes of sizes $k_1,k_2,\dots$ has exactly $k_1^2+k_2^2+\cdots$ ordered pairs (every pair inside a class).
So the size is $3^2+1^2=10$.
Any equivalence relation containing $(1,2),(1,3)$ must put $1,2,3$ in one class, so this is the smallest: $10$.

useful_results: Smallest equivalence relation containing a set of pairs = partition into connected components of the graph formed by those pairs.
If the classes have sizes $k_1,\dots,k_r$ then $|R|=\sum k_i^2$ (with $\sum k_i=n$).
Number of equivalence relations on an $n$-set = Bell number ($1,2,5,15,52,\dots$); for $n=4$ there are $15$.

questions.question: Consider the relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ defined as $a\,R_1\,b\iff a^2+b^2=1$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $(a,b)\,R_2\,(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c$ for all $(a,b),(c,d)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Then:
options: Neither $R_1$ nor $R_2$ is an equivalence relation
questions.answer: (C) Only R₂ is an equivalence relation
questions.key_idea: $R_1$ fails reflexivity at once; $R_2$ passes all three tests, transitivity by adding the two given equations.
solution: $R_1$: $a\,R_1\,a$ would need $2a^2=1$, which is false for $a=0$ (for example). So $R_1$ is not reflexive and hence not an equivalence relation.
$R_2$ reflexive: $(a,b)\,R_2\,(a,b)\iff a+b=b+a$, which is true.
$R_2$ symmetric: $(a,b)\,R_2\,(c,d)$ gives $a+d=b+c$, i.e. $d+a=c+b$, i.e. $c+b=d+a$, so $(c,d)\,R_2\,(a,b)$.
Adding (1) and (2): $a+d+c+f=b+c+d+e$, so $a+f=b+e$, i.e. $(a,b)\,R_2\,(e,f)$.
So $R_2$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, an equivalence relation, while $R_1$ is not: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: $a+d=b+c$ is the same as $a-b=c-d$: $R_2$ relates pairs with equal value of $f(a,b)=a-b$, and any such relation is automatically an equivalence.
solution: Rewrite $a+d=b+c$ as $a-b=c-d$. Define $f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ by $f(a,b)=a-b$.
Then $(a,b)\,R_2\,(c,d)\iff f(a,b)=f(c,d)$.
Equality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so $R_2$ inherits all three properties: it is an equivalence relation (its classes are the fibres of $f$, one for each integer difference).
For $R_1$: take $a=0$; $0^2+0^2=0\ne1$, so $(0,0)\notin R_1$ and $R_1$ is not reflexive.
Hence only $R_2$ is an equivalence relation: (C).

useful_results: Any relation of the form '$f(x)=f(y)$' is an equivalence relation; its classes are the fibres $f^{-1}(c)$. Always try to rewrite the defining condition in this form.
$a+d=b+c\iff a-b=c-d$ (difference classes), $ad=bc\iff a/b=c/d$ (ratio classes, for non-zero $b,d$).
Disproving an equivalence relation needs only one failure; check reflexivity first, it is the quickest to break (here $a^2+a^2=1$ fails).

concepts: Counting subsets with no two consecutive elements
questions.question: For $n\ge2$, let $S_n$ denote the set of all subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ with no two consecutive numbers. For example $\{1,3,5\}\in S_6$ but $\{1,2,4\}\notin S_6$. Then $n(S_5)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The number of $r$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no two consecutive is $\binom{n-r+1}{r}$.
solution: The number of $r$-element subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ with no two consecutive numbers is $\binom{n-r+1}{r}$.
For $n=5$ the size $r$ ranges over $0,1,2,3$, because three non-consecutive numbers fit but four do not.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split on whether $n$ is in the subset: this gives the Fibonacci recurrence $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$.
solution: Let $a_n$ be the number of valid subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (the empty set counts). Then $a_0=1$ and $a_1=2$.
If $n$ is not chosen, the rest is any valid subset of $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$: $a_{n-1}$ ways.
If $n$ is chosen, then $n-1$ cannot be, and the rest is any valid subset of $\{1,\dots,n-2\}$: $a_{n-2}$ ways.
Hence $n(S_5)=13$.

useful_results: The number of subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no two consecutive elements is the Fibonacci number $F_{n+2}$ ($1,2,3,5,8,13,\dots$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$), and $\sum_r\binom{n-r+1}{r}=F_{n+2}$.
Choosing $r$ non-adjacent items from $n$ in a line: $\binom{n-r+1}{r}$ (place the $r$ items in the $n-r+1$ gaps created by the $n-r$ unchosen ones).
On a circle (first and last also adjacent) the count of $r$-subsets is $\frac{n}{n-r}\binom{n-r}{r}$ and the total is the Lucas number $L_n$ (here $L_5=11$).

questions.question: The number of relations on the set $A=\{1,2,3\}$, containing at most $6$ elements including $(1,2)$, which are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Reflexivity and $(1,2)$ fix four pairs; then count the transitive additions from the other five pairs, separately for $4$, $5$ and $6$ elements.
solution: $A\times A$ has $9$ pairs. Reflexivity and the given pair force $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2)$ into $R$.
The remaining possible pairs are $(1,3),(2,1),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2)$; we add some of them keeping $R$ transitive and not symmetric, with $|R|\le6$.
Case I: exactly $4$ elements: $R$ is just the four forced pairs. It is transitive and not symmetric, so this gives $1$ relation.

Case II: exactly $5$ elements: add one pair. $(1,3)$ and $(3,2)$ each keep $R$ transitive; $(2,1)$ makes $R$ symmetric (an equivalence relation, excluded); $(2,3)$ forces $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$ forces $(3,2)$, so they need $6$ elements. This gives $2$ relations.
Case III: exactly $6$ elements: the valid pairs of additions are $\{(2,3),(1,3)\}$, $\{(1,3),(3,2)\}$ and $\{(3,1),(3,2)\}$. This gives $3$ relations.
Total $=1+2+3=6$. (The PDF's answer key prints $5$, but its own working ends with $6$, and a brute-force check gives $6$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Classify by the poset structure of the equivalence classes: a reflexive transitive relation is a partial order on classes; count the shapes with $1\le2$ that have at most $6$ pairs.
solution: A reflexive transitive relation is a preorder: elements that are related both ways form a class, and classes are ordered. It is not symmetric exactly when some pair is related only one way.

If $1,2$ stay in separate classes (no $(2,1)$), the relation is a partial order on $\{1,2,3\}$ with $1<2$. Place $3$: (i) unrelated to both, $4$ pairs; (ii) $1<3$ only, $5$ pairs; (iii) $3<2$ only, $5$ pairs; (iv) $1<2<3$, $6$ pairs; (v) $1<3<2$, $6$ pairs; (vi) $3<1<2$, $6$ pairs. That is $6$ relations, all with at most $6$ pairs.

If $1,2$ are in one class (with $(2,1)$), the class $\{1,2\}$ has $4$ pairs and $3$ is either separate (that is symmetric, excluded), above it (needs $(1,3),(2,3)$: $7$ pairs), below it ($7$ pairs), or merged (all $9$, symmetric).
So the only candidates are the six partial orders above: the answer is $6$.

useful_results: Reflexive + transitive = preorder (quasi-order). Elements related both ways form classes; the classes carry a partial order. Preorders on $3$ labelled elements: $29$.
Reflexive, transitive and symmetric together is an equivalence relation; so 'not symmetric' means: not all comparable pairs are mutual.

When counting relations with a size cap, build from the forced pairs ($n$ diagonal pairs plus the given ones) and list transitive extensions by size; always check closure under composition after each addition.
Never trust a printed key blindly: here the key (5) disagrees with its own working (6).

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$. The number of relations on $A$, containing $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$, which are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Transitivity forces $(1,3)$, so the base relation is the chain $1\to2\to3$; only the reverse pairs can be added.
solution: $R$ is reflexive, so it contains $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)$, and it contains $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$.
Transitivity applied to $(1,2),(2,3)$ forces $(1,3)$ as well. So the smallest such relation is $R_1=\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)\}$, which is not symmetric.
Add $(3,2)$: $R_2=R_1\cup\{(3,2)\}$ is transitive, and not symmetric because $(1,2)\in R_2$ but $(2,1)\notin R_2$.
Add $(2,1)$: $R_3=R_1\cup\{(2,1)\}$ is transitive, and not symmetric because $(2,3)\in R_3$ but $(3,2)\notin R_3$.
Adding $(3,1)$ forces $(3,2)$ and $(2,1)$ as well, and adding both $(2,1)$ and $(3,2)$ forces $(3,1)$; both give the full relation $A\times A$, which is symmetric, so they are excluded.
Hence there are $3$ such relations: $R_1,R_2,R_3$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's list shows R3 = {(1,2),(2,3),(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(2,1)} without (1,3). That set is not transitive ((1,2),(2,3) force (1,3)), so R3 as printed is not valid; the correct R3 must also contain (1,3). The PDF's list for R2 also omits (1,3). The count 3 is right. Also added the reason why other additions are excluded.

alternate_solutions.idea: View $1\le2\le3$ as a chain with two links; each link is either left one-way or collapsed into mutual (both-ways), and collapsing both makes everything symmetric.
solution: Reflexive and transitive containing $(1,2),(2,3)$ means $1\preceq2\preceq3$ and so $1\preceq3$: a chain.

The only extra pairs that can still be added without forcing symmetry of unrelated things are the reverses of the chain relations: $(2,1)$ (collapse link $1\!-\!2$) and $(3,2)$ (collapse link $2\!-\!3$).
Each link is independently kept one-way or collapsed: $2\times2=4$ relations.
If both links collapse, $1\sim2\sim3$ and $R=A\times A$, which is symmetric: remove it.
Adding $(3,1)$ alone is impossible: it forces $(3,2)$ and $(2,1)$, i.e. both links collapse.
So $4-1=3$ relations.

useful_results: If $R$ is transitive and contains $a\to b\to c$ it contains $a\to c$: always close the forced pairs first.
Preorders containing a chain $x_1\preceq x_2\preceq\dots\preceq x_k$ correspond to choosing which links are collapsed (made mutual); collapsing a whole chain makes it an equivalence class.
Mutual pair $(a,b),(b,a)$ together with $(b,c)$ forces $(a,c)$: collapsing propagates, so check closure after every addition.

questions.question: In a survey of $220$ students of a higher secondary school, it was found that at least $125$ and at most $130$ students studied Mathematics; at least $85$ and at most $95$ studied Physics; at least $75$ and at most $90$ studied Chemistry; $30$ studied both Physics and Chemistry; $50$ studied both Chemistry and Mathematics; $40$ studied both Mathematics and Physics and $10$ studied none of these subjects. Let $m$ and $n$ respectively be the least and the most number of students who studied all the three subjects. Then $m+n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Fill the Venn diagram with $x$ in the middle; the total gives $x$ from the subject totals, and no region may be negative.
solution: Let $x$ be the number who studied all three subjects. The pair-only regions are $M\cap P$ only $=40-x$, $P\cap C$ only $=30-x$, $C\cap M$ only $=50-x$.
$220-10=210$ students study at least one subject, so the seven regions add to $210$.
Smallest totals ($M=125$, $P=85$, $C=75$): single regions are $M$ only $=35+x$, $P$ only $=15+x$, $C$ only $=x-5$.
Sum of regions: $(35+x)+(15+x)+(x-5)+(40-x)+(30-x)+(50-x)+x=165+x$. Setting this equal to $210$ gives $x=45$.

But $30-x\ge0$ requires $x\le30$, so $x=45$ is impossible: the smallest totals cannot give $210$ students; the greatest value possible is $x=30$ (a valid case, for example $M=125$, $P=85$, $C=90$). Hence $n=30$.
Largest totals ($M=130$, $P=95$, $C=90$): $M$ only $=40+x$, $P$ only $=25+x$, $C$ only $=10+x$.
Sum of regions: $(40+x)+(25+x)+(10+x)+(40-x)+(30-x)+(50-x)+x=195+x$. Setting this equal to $210$ gives $x=15$, and all regions are non-negative. Hence $m=15$.
Therefore $m+n=15+30=45$.
questions.correction_note: PDF labels the two cases the wrong way round (it writes 'x = 30 = m' and 'x = 15 = n') and states 'x = 45' from the first diagram, then jumps to 30 without saying why (pair-only region 30-x cannot be negative). Also its second diagram total reads 205+x=220 (including the 10 outside), which is the same as 195+x=210. Correct: least m = 15, most n = 30; the sum 45 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the inclusion–exclusion formula directly: $x=210-(M+P+C)+120$ gives a range from the subject totals, and $x\le$ every pairwise overlap caps it.
solution: Inclusion–exclusion: $210=M+P+C-(40+30+50)+x$, so $x=330-(M+P+C)$.
Also $x$ cannot exceed any pairwise overlap: $x\le\min(40,30,50)=30$. So $15\le x\le30$.
Both ends are attainable: $x=15$ with $(M,P,C)=(130,95,90)$ and $x=30$ with $(125,85,90)$; in each case every Venn region is non-negative.
Hence $m=15$, $n=30$ and $m+n=45$.

useful_results: Three sets: $|A\cup B\cup C|=\sum|A|-\sum|A\cap B|+|A\cap B\cap C|$, so the triple overlap is $x=|\cup|-\sum|A|+\sum|A\cap B|$.
Bounds on $x$ come from two places: the range of the totals, and non-negativity of every Venn region (in particular $x\le$ each pairwise intersection).
Always check that an extreme value from one condition satisfies all other region constraints before accepting it.

questions.question: Let $A=\{2,3,6,7\}$ and $B=\{4,5,6,8\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A\times B$ defined by $(a_1,b_1)\,R\,(a_2,b_2)$ if and only if $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2$. Then the number of elements in $R$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Count ordered pairs of elements of $A\times B$ (16 elements) with $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2$, systematically by first element.
solution: $A\times B$ has $16$ elements; $R$ consists of the ordered pairs $((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2))$ with $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2$. List the partners of each first element.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite the condition as $a_1-b_1=-(a_2-b_2)$: group elements by their difference $d=a-b$ and count pairs of opposite differences.
solution: Number of ordered pairs $=\sum_d N(d)N(-d)$.
$d=0$: $1\cdot1=1$. $d=\pm1$: $2\cdot2+2\cdot2=8$. $d=\pm2$: $3\cdot2+2\cdot3=12$. $d=\pm3$: $2\cdot1+1\cdot2=4$. Differences $\pm4,\pm5,\pm6$ have no opposite partner.

useful_results: A condition $f(p)+f(q)=0$ (or $f(p)=g(q)$) on pairs is counted as $\sum_v N(v)\,N(-v)$ from the frequency table of $f$ - a single pass instead of testing all $n^2$ pairs.
$a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2\iff a_1-b_1=b_2-a_2$: a sum condition on two coordinates becomes a difference-matching condition.
Note this relation is symmetric but not reflexive in general (only $(6,6)$ is related to itself).

concepts: Sets of ordered pairs of natural numbers
questions.question: Let the set $C=\{(x,y)\mid x^2-2^y=2023,\ x,y\in\mathbb{N}\}$. Then $\sum_{(x,y)\in C}(x+y)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Show $C$ has exactly one point: $x^2\equiv7\pmod8$ is impossible, so $2^y$ must be small ($y=1$ or $2$).
solution: The equation is $x^2-2^y=2023$ with $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$.
We must make sure there is no other solution, because the sum runs over all of $C$.
For $y\ge3$: $2^y\equiv0\pmod8$ and $2023=8\cdot252+7\equiv7\pmod8$, so $x^2\equiv7\pmod8$. But squares are $\equiv0,1,4\pmod8$, so no solution.
questions.correction_note: The PDF only states 'x^2 - 2^y = 2023 => x = 45, y = 1' and the sum 46, with no argument that (45,1) is the only solution (needed because the sum is over the whole set). The mod 8 argument and the y = 2 check were added. The answer 46 is correct. Note: the PDF's text layer shows 'x^2 - 2y'; the page image shows 2^y.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract $45^2$: $x^2-45^2=2^y-2$, so $(x-45)(x+45)=2(2^{y-1}-1)$, and a parity count of factors of $2$ shows $y=1$.
solution: Now $x^2=2023+2^y$ is odd, so $x$ is odd and both $x-45$ and $x+45$ are even: the left side is divisible by $4$.
For $y\ge2$, $2^{y-1}-1$ is odd, so the right side is $2\times$ odd, not divisible by $4$. Contradiction. So $y=1$.
Hence the sum is $45+1=46$.

useful_results: For equations $x^2-2^y=N$: reduce modulo $8$ (squares are $0,1,4$) to kill all large $y$, then test the few small cases.
Squares mod $8\in\{0,1,4\}$; squares mod $3\in\{0,1\}$; squares mod $4\in\{0,1\}$ - the standard tools to prove an exponential Diophantine equation has no solution or only small ones.
Spotting the nearest square ($2025=45^2$) and rewriting as a difference of squares $(x-a)(x+a)$ turns the equation into a factoring problem.

questions.question: A group of $40$ students appeared in an examination of $3$ subjects - Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry. It was found that all students passed in at least one of the subjects, $20$ students passed in Mathematics, $25$ students passed in Physics, $16$ students passed in Chemistry, at most $11$ students passed in both Mathematics and Physics, at most $15$ students passed in both Physics and Chemistry, at most $15$ students passed in both Mathematics and Chemistry. The maximum number of students passed in all three subjects is ______.
questions.key_idea: The triple overlap cannot exceed any pairwise overlap, and the union formula ties the pairwise overlaps to $x$.
solution: Let $x$ be the number who passed all three subjects. Then $x\le|M\cap P|\le11$, so $11-x\ge0$ and $x\le11$.
Test $x=11$: then $|M\cap P|=11$ exactly. Inclusion–exclusion: $40=20+25+16-(|M\cap P|+|P\cap C|+|M\cap C|)+x$, so the three pairwise overlaps add to $21+x=32$.
So $|P\cap C|+|M\cap C|=32-11=21$, but each of them is at least $x=11$, so their sum is at least $22>21$. Contradiction: $x=11$ does not satisfy the data.
Test $x=10$: the pairwise overlaps add to $31$; take $|M\cap P|=10$, $|P\cap C|=11$, $|M\cap C|=10$ (each at least $10$ and within the bounds).
Then $M$ only $=20-10-10+10=10$, $P$ only $=25-10-11+10=14$, $C$ only $=16-11-10+10=5$: all non-negative and the regions add to $40$.
Hence the maximum number of students passing all three subjects is $10$. (The PDF's printed key shows $11$, but the PDF's own working and the NTA answer give $10$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Each pairwise overlap is at least $x$, so the pairwise sum $21+x$ from inclusion–exclusion must be at least $3x$: this gives $x\le10.5$ immediately.
solution: Inclusion–exclusion with all students in the union: $40=61-S+x$, where $S=|M\cap P|+|P\cap C|+|M\cap C|$. So $S=21+x$.
Each pairwise overlap contains the triple overlap, so $S\ge3x$.
Hence $21+x\ge3x$, so $x\le10.5$, and $x\le10$ as $x$ is an integer.
Check $x=10$ is attainable: $S=31$ with $(|M\cap P|,|P\cap C|,|M\cap C|)=(10,11,10)$ satisfies the caps $11,15,15$ and gives non-negative regions ($10,14,5$ for single-subject only).
So the maximum is $10$.

useful_results: $|A\cap B\cap C|\le\min$ of the pairwise intersections, and $\sum|A\cap B|\ge3|A\cap B\cap C|$: a quick upper bound for the triple overlap.
Union formula rearranged: $|A\cap B|+|B\cap C|+|C\cap A|=\sum|A|-|A\cup B\cup C|+|A\cap B\cap C|$.
Always confirm the extreme value is attainable; a bound from one inequality (here $x\le11$) can be loose.

questions.question: The number of symmetric relations defined on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ which are not reflexive is ______.
questions.key_idea: A symmetric relation on an $n$-set is a choice among $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ independent slots (diagonal pairs and unordered off-diagonal pairs).
solution: For $n=4$, a symmetric relation is determined by choosing, independently, each of the $4$ diagonal pairs and each of the $\binom42=6$ unordered off-diagonal pairs (with both orders together).
So the number of symmetric relations is $2^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}=2^{10}=1024$.
A symmetric relation that is also reflexive must contain all $4$ diagonal pairs, leaving only the $6$ off-diagonal choices free: $2^{\frac{n^2-n}{2}}=2^{6}=64$.
Symmetric relations that are not reflexive $=2^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}-2^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}$ with $n=4$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes '(n = 5)' next to the formula 2^{n(n+1)/2} - 2^{n(n-1)/2}, but the set has 4 elements, so n = 4. It then evaluates 1024 - 64, which is the n = 4 value (n = 5 would give 32768 - 1024). The numbers and the answer 960 are correct; only the printed 'n = 5' is a slip.

alternate_solutions.idea: Not reflexive means at least one diagonal pair is missing: choose which diagonal pairs are missing, and the off-diagonal pairs are free.
solution: The relation is symmetric, so the $6$ unordered off-diagonal pairs can be included or excluded freely: $2^6=64$ ways.
Not reflexive means a non-empty set of diagonal pairs $(i,i)$ is absent. The set of absent diagonal pairs is a non-empty subset of $\{1,2,3,4\}$: $2^4-1=15$ choices.
Total $=15\times64=960$.

useful_results: Symmetric relations on an $n$-set: $2^{n(n+1)/2}$; reflexive and symmetric: $2^{n(n-1)/2}$; so symmetric but not reflexive: $2^{n(n+1)/2}-2^{n(n-1)/2}=(2^n-1)\,2^{n(n-1)/2}$.
Other counts on an $n$-set: all relations $2^{n^2}$; reflexive $2^{n^2-n}$; anti-symmetric $2^n\,3^{n(n-1)/2}$.

concepts: Equivalence relations: smallest equivalence relation containing a given relation
questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $R=\{(1,2),(2,3),(1,4)\}$ be a relation on $A$. Let $S$ be the equivalence relation on $A$ such that $R\subset S$ and the number of elements in $S$ is $n$. Then, the minimum value of $n$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: All four elements are linked through $1$, so the smallest equivalence relation is a single class and has $4^2$ pairs.
solution: For reflexivity add $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)$: $4$ new pairs.
For symmetry add the reverses of the given pairs: $(2,1),(3,2),(4,1)$: $3$ new pairs.
Total pairs added $=4+3+6=13$, and $|R|=3$.
So the minimum number of elements in $S$ is $3+13=16$ (which is $4^2$, all of $A\times A$).
questions.correction_note: PDF lists the symmetric additions as (2,1), (4,1), (3,1). The reverse of (2,3) is (3,2), not (3,1); (3,1) arises later from transitivity (and is listed there too). The corrected symmetric additions are (2,1), (3,2), (4,1). The counts (4 + 3 + 6 = 13 added, 16 in total) are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Smallest equivalence relation = connected components of the graph of $R$; one component of size $4$ gives $4^2=16$ pairs.
solution: Draw edges $1-2$, $2-3$, $1-4$ on the vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ (direction does not matter for the equivalence closure).
The graph is connected (a path $3-2-1-4$), so there is a single equivalence class $\{1,2,3,4\}$.
An equivalence relation with one class of size $4$ is $A\times A$, with $4^2=16$ elements.
Any equivalence relation containing $R$ must merge all four elements, so $16$ is forced: $n_{\min}=16$.

useful_results: Equivalence closure of $R$: connected components of its graph; the size is $\sum(\text{class size})^2$.
A connected graph on $n$ vertices (a tree needs $n-1$ edges) forces the full relation $A\times A$, with $n^2$ pairs.
Compare the cost: pairs to add $=n^2-|R|=16-3=13$.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\dots,100\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A$ defined by $(x,y)\in R$ if and only if $2x=3y$. Let $R_1$ be a symmetric relation on $A$ such that $R\subset R_1$ and the number of elements in $R_1$ is $n$. Then, the minimum value of $n$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: The smallest symmetric relation containing $R$ adds the reverse of each pair; no pair of $R$ is the reverse of another.
solution: $2x=3y$ means $x=3k$, $y=2k$ for a positive integer $k$, with $3k\le100$, i.e. $k\le33$.
A symmetric $R_1\supset R$ must also contain the reverse $(2,3),(4,6),\dots,(66,99)$ of each pair.
The reverse $(y,x)$ of a pair of $R$ is never in $R$ ($2y=3x$ together with $2x=3y$ gives $x=y=0$), so the $33$ reverses are all new.
The smallest such relation has $33+33=66$ elements, so the minimum value of $n$ is $66$.
useful_results: Smallest symmetric relation containing $R$ is $R\cup R^{-1}$, of size $|R|+|R^{-1}|-|R\cap R^{-1}|=2|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$.
Here $R\cap R^{-1}=\emptyset$ (a pair of $R$ and its reverse would force $x=y=0$), so the size is $2\cdot33$.
Linear conditions $px=qy$ on $\{1,\dots,N\}$: solutions $(qk,pk)$ with $qk\le N$ and $pk\le N$, so $\lfloor N/\max(p,q)\rfloor$ of them.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\dots,20\}$. Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be two relations on $A$ such that $R_1=\{(a,b): b \text{ is divisible by } a\}$ and $R_2=\{(a,b): a \text{ is an integral multiple of } b\}$. Then, the number of elements in $R_1-R_2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $R_2$ is the reverse of $R_1$, so $R_1\cap R_2$ is only the diagonal and $R_1-R_2$ is the set of strict divisibility pairs.
solution: Count by $a$: $\lfloor20/a\rfloor$ multiples, i.e. $20+10+6+5+4+3+2+2+2+2+1\cdot10=66$ ordered pairs in $R_1$.
$R_1\cap R_2$ consists of pairs with $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$, i.e. $a=b$: $\{(1,1),\dots,(20,20)\}$, which is $20$ pairs.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count the same pairs by the second coordinate: each $b$ contributes its proper divisors, $d(b)-1$ of them.
solution: $R_1-R_2$ is the set of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\mid b$ and $a\ne b$, i.e. $a$ is a proper divisor of $b$.
For each $b$ the number of such $a$ is $d(b)-1$, where $d(b)$ is the number of divisors of $b$.

useful_results: $\#\{(a,b):a\mid b,\ 1\le a,b\le N\}=\sum_{a\le N}\lfloor N/a\rfloor=\sum_{b\le N}d(b)$ (counting by multiples = counting by divisors). For $N=20$ this is $66$.
$R^{-1}$ swaps coordinates: here $R_2=R_1^{-1}$, and $R\cap R^{-1}$ is the 'symmetric part' (only the diagonal for divisibility, since $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$ force $a=b$).
Divisibility is reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive: a partial order, not an equivalence.

concepts: Types of relations: reflexive, symmetric and transitive
questions.question: Let $A$ be the set of all functions $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ and $R$ be a relation on $A$ such that $R=\{(f,g): f(0)=g(1)\text{ and }f(1)=g(0)\}$. Then $R$ is:
options: Reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
Symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
Transitive but neither reflexive nor symmetric
Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
questions.answer: (B) Symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
questions.key_idea: $(f,f)\in R$ needs $f(0)=f(1)$; swap roles for symmetry; for transitivity chain $f\,R\,g\,R\,h$ and compare with what $f\,R\,h$ needs.
solution: Reflexive: $(f,f)\in R$ would need $f(0)=f(1)$ and $f(1)=f(0)$. This is not true for every function (e.g. $f(x)=x$), so $R$ is not reflexive.
Symmetric: let $(f,g)\in R$, so $f(0)=g(1)$ and $f(1)=g(0)$.
Then $g(0)=f(1)$ and $g(1)=f(0)$, which is exactly the condition for $(g,f)\in R$. So $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive: let $(f,g)\in R$ and $(g,h)\in R$: $f(0)=g(1)$, $f(1)=g(0)$ and $g(0)=h(1)$, $g(1)=h(0)$.
These give $f(0)=g(1)=h(0)$ and $f(1)=g(0)=h(1)$.
For $(f,h)\in R$ we would need $f(0)=h(1)$ and $f(1)=h(0)$, which does not follow (it would need $f(0)=f(1)$).
So $R$ is not transitive. Hence $R$ is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: If $R$ were transitive, symmetry would give $fRg$ and $gRf\Rightarrow fRf$, which is false whenever $f(0)\ne f(1)$ - a one-line contradiction.
solution: Take $f(x)=x$, so $f(0)=0\ne1=f(1)$; then $(f,f)\notin R$ and $R$ is not reflexive.
Take $g(x)=1-x$: $f(0)=0=g(1)$ and $f(1)=1=g(0)$, so $f\,R\,g$; and symmetry (swap the equations) gives $g\,R\,f$.
If $R$ were transitive, $f\,R\,g$ and $g\,R\,f$ would give $f\,R\,f$, which is false. So $R$ is not transitive, and it is symmetric.
Hence (B).

useful_results: A symmetric and transitive relation is reflexive on every element that is related to anything: $aRb$, $bRa\Rightarrow aRa$. So 'symmetric and transitive but not reflexive' needs some element related to nothing.
Hence a symmetric relation where every element has a partner but some element is not related to itself cannot be transitive (use this to disprove transitivity fast).
For relations 'twisted' by a swap of arguments (like $f(0)=g(1),\ f(1)=g(0)$), symmetry is automatic and reflexivity fails.

questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10+3x-x^2}}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+|x|}}$ is $(a,b)$, then $(1+a)^2+b^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Each term needs a strictly positive quantity under its root; intersect the two conditions.
solution: $x+|x|=2x$ for $x\ge0$ and $0$ for $x<0$.
So $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+|x|}}$ is defined only when $x+|x|>0$, i.e. $x>0$ (as $2x>0$).
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10+3x-x^2}}$ is defined when $10+3x-x^2>0$, i.e. $x^2-3x-10<0$.
Domain $=(0,\infty)\cap(-2,5)=(0,5)$, so $a=0$ and $b=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square: $10+3x-x^2=\frac{49}{4}-(x-\frac32)^2$, so the first condition says $|x-\frac32|<\frac72$; and $x+|x|=2\max(x,0)$.
solution: $10+3x-x^2=\frac{49}{4}-\left(x-\frac32\right)^2>0\iff\left|x-\frac32\right|<\frac72$, i.e. $-2<x<5$.
$x+|x|=2\max(x,0)$, which is positive exactly when $x>0$.
The two conditions together give $0<x<5$: $(a,b)=(0,5)$.

useful_results: $x+|x|=2x^+$ ($=2x$ if $x\ge0$, else $0$): positive only for $x>0$. Similarly $|x|-x>0$ only for $x<0$.
A quadratic $c+bx-ax^2>0$ holds between its roots; completing the square turns it into $|x-h|<r$.
A term $1/\sqrt{g(x)}$ needs $g(x)>0$ (strict), while $\sqrt{g(x)}$ alone needs $g(x)\ge0$.

questions.question: Let $f$ be a function such that $f(x)+3f\!\left(\dfrac{24}{x}\right)=4x$, $x\ne0$. Then $f(3)+f(8)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Since $\frac{24}{3}=8$ and $\frac{24}{8}=3$, substituting $x=3$ and $x=8$ gives two equations in $f(3),f(8)$.
solution: Given $f(x)+3f\!\left(\frac{24}{x}\right)=4x$.
Hence $f(3)+f(8)=11$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace $x$ by $\frac{24}{x}$ to get a second equation for all $x$, solve for $f(x)$ explicitly, and evaluate.
solution: Replacing $x$ by $\frac{24}{x}$: $f\!\left(\frac{24}{x}\right)+3f(x)=\frac{96}{x}$.
With $f(x)+3f\!\left(\frac{24}{x}\right)=4x$, eliminate $f\!\left(\frac{24}{x}\right)$: $9f(x)-f(x)=\frac{288}{x}-4x$, so $f(x)=\frac{36}{x}-\frac{x}{2}$.
$f(3)+f(8)=\frac{21}{2}+\frac12=11$. (This also shows such an $f$ exists.)

useful_results: For $f(x)+a\,f(\sigma(x))=h(x)$ with an involution $\sigma$ ($\sigma(\sigma(x))=x$): replacing $x$ by $\sigma(x)$ gives a second equation, and $f(x)=\dfrac{h(x)-a\,h(\sigma(x))}{1-a^2}$ when $a^2\ne1$.
Here $\sigma(x)=24/x$, $a=3$, $h(x)=4x$: $f(x)=\dfrac{4x-3\cdot96/x}{-8}=\dfrac{36}{x}-\dfrac x2$.
Adding the two equations at $x$ and $\sigma(x)$ gives $(1+a)\,(f(x)+f(\sigma(x)))=h(x)+h(\sigma(x))$: here $4\,(f(3)+f(8))=12+32$.

questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\log_7\big(1-\log_4(x^2-9x+18)\big)$ is $(\alpha,\beta)\cup(\gamma,\delta)$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Two nested logarithms need $x^2-9x+18>0$ and $1-\log_4(x^2-9x+18)>0$, i.e. $0<x^2-9x+18<4$.
solution: $f$ is defined when $1-\log_4(x^2-9x+18)>0$ (and the inner argument $x^2-9x+18>0$).
Intersection: $(\alpha,\beta)\cup(\gamma,\delta)=(2,3)\cup(6,7)$.
$\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=2+3+6+7=18$: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: The quadratic is symmetric about $x=\frac92$, so the domain is symmetric about $\frac92$ and the endpoints pair up to sums of $9$.
solution: $x^2-9x+18=\left(x-\frac92\right)^2-\frac94$. Let $t=\left|x-\frac92\right|$.
The condition $0<x^2-9x+18<4$ becomes $\frac94<t^2<\frac{25}{4}$, i.e. $\frac32<t<\frac52$.
So $x\in\left(\frac92-\frac52,\ \frac92-\frac32\right)\cup\left(\frac92+\frac32,\ \frac92+\frac52\right)=(2,3)\cup(6,7)$.
The endpoints pair as $2+7=9$ and $3+6=9$ (reflection in $x=\frac92$), so the sum is $9+9=18$.

useful_results: For $\log_a(1-\log_b g(x))$: need $g>0$ and $\log_b g<1$, i.e. $0<g<b$ when $b>1$ (reverse the inequality if $0<b<1$).
The domain of a function of a quadratic $g(x)$ is symmetric about the vertex $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$; for $g=x^2-9x+18$ the sum of the endpoints of mirror intervals is $9$.
Compose conditions inside-out: the inner log needs a positive argument, then the outer log needs its argument positive.

questions.question: Let $f,g:(1,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+3}{5x+2}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{2-3x}{1-x}$. If the range of the function $f\circ g:[2,4]\to\mathbb{R}$ is $[\alpha,\beta]$, then $\dfrac{1}{\beta-\alpha}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $f\circ g$ is a Möbius function, monotonic on $[2,4]$, so the range is the interval between its end values.
solution: Numerator: $2\cdot\dfrac{2-3x}{1-x}+3=\dfrac{4-6x+3-3x}{1-x}=\dfrac{7-9x}{1-x}$. Denominator: $5\cdot\dfrac{2-3x}{1-x}+2=\dfrac{10-15x+2-2x}{1-x}=\dfrac{12-17x}{1-x}$.
So $f(g(x))=\dfrac{7-9x}{12-17x}=\dfrac{9x-7}{17x-12}$, which on its own takes every real value except $\frac{9}{17}$.
On the domain $[2,4]$ the function is a continuous monotonic graph (a branch of a hyperbola with vertical asymptote $x=\frac{12}{17}$, outside $[2,4]$), so the range is between the end values.
The range is $\left[\frac12,\frac{29}{56}\right]$, so $\alpha=\frac12$, $\beta=\frac{29}{56}$.
$\beta-\alpha=\dfrac{29}{56}-\dfrac{28}{56}=\dfrac{1}{56}$, so $\dfrac{1}{\beta-\alpha}=56$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Compose the two Möbius maps by multiplying their matrices, then use the sign of the determinant to see monotonicity.
solution: A function $\dfrac{px+q}{rx+s}$ corresponds to the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}$, and composition corresponds to matrix product.

$f\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$, $g\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}-3&2\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $f\circ g\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\5&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-3&2\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-9&7\\-17&12\end{pmatrix}$.

A Möbius map $\frac{px+q}{rx+s}$ has derivative $\frac{ps-qr}{(rx+s)^2}$, so a positive determinant means increasing wherever defined; hence $f\circ g$ is increasing on $[2,4]$ and the range is $[f(g(2)),f(g(4))]=\left[\frac12,\frac{29}{56}\right]$.
$\dfrac{1}{\beta-\alpha}=\dfrac{1}{1/56}=56$.

useful_results: Möbius (linear fractional) maps $\frac{px+q}{rx+s}$ compose like $2\times2$ matrices; the derivative is $\frac{ps-qr}{(rx+s)^2}$, so the sign of $ps-qr$ decides increasing/decreasing on each side of the pole.
Range of a monotonic continuous function on $[a,b]$ is the interval between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$; just check that the pole $x=-\frac sr$ is outside $[a,b]$ (here $\frac{12}{17}$).
Alternative form: $\frac{9x-7}{17x-12}=\frac{9}{17}-\frac{11}{17(17x-12)}$ - a shifted reciprocal, easy to see as increasing.
